children: To extend the reach of its global lending, the World Bank is increasingly turning to help from an outside ally: the private sector.

The bank is still investing its own funds at scale. But in recent years, the bank also has marshaled capital investments from the private sector at an unprecedented clip, according to new data it published Thursday.

In the fiscal year that ran through June, the World Bank mobilized $112 billion in private capital, alongside the $123 billion of its own financing that it advanced. That marks a sea change from five years ago, when $92.5 billion of World Bank financing was paired with $24.4 billion of private capital.
The World Bank makes loans to support infrastructure, business development and other projects in developing countries. It is owned and backed by member countries.

The shift reflects a marquee World Bank initiative under its president since 2023, Ajay Banga, a former CEO of Mastercard. Banga said that global-development finance needs exceed the World Bank's own funding sources by so much that bringing in more private partners has become a necessity.

The World Bank's backing from member countries allows for a significant volume of lending on its own. "But even with that, you don't have enough money," Banga said. "So you come around to the issue that the only real way to get consistent, solid flows of money to come into the developing world is through the private capital system."

Under the approach, the World Bank has turned more to funding and expertise from private-sector builders and operators. It has upped its outreach to managers that control large pools of capital-from public pension funds to insurers and asset managers. More often in recent years, the funds that the World Bank advances have been intended not only to jump-start projects but also to seed parallel investments from the private sector, lifting the development bank's impact.

Recent World Bank projects tapping private funding include working with mining giant Rio Tinto to develop a lithium mine planned for Salta, Argentina, and a new investment partnership with Banco Industrial, a Guatemalan bank, aimed at lending to micro, small and medium-size enterprises. The lithium-mine investment matched $400 million in World Bank capital with $775 million raised from private investors.

To work better with private-sector investors, the World Bank has increasingly shifted to a playbook that looks more like Wall Street's. In recent weeks, the Washington, D.C.-based lender has opened offices in New York City, and it is expanding in other global financial capitals.

The World Bank also has boosted its capability to insure private-sector investors against political and other risks. In addition, it is increasingly offering investors securitized products that give them exposure to broad packages of projects at once.
